question.text: Can elevated troponin I levels predict complicated clinical course and inhospital mortality in patients with acute pulmonary embolism?
question.context: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the value of elevated cardiac troponin I (cTnI) for prediction of complicated clinical course and in-hospital mortality in patients with confirmed acute pulmonary embolism (PE). This study was a retrospective chart review of patients diagnosed as having PE, in whom cTnI testing was obtained at emergency department (ED) presentation between January 2002 and April 2006. Clinical characteristics; echocardiographic right ventricular dysfunction; inhospital mortality; and adverse clinical events including need for inotropic support, mechanical ventilation, and thrombolysis were compared in patients with elevated cTnI levels vs patients with normal cTnI levels. One hundred sixteen patients with PE were identified, and 77 of them (66%) were included in the study. Thirty-three patients (42%) had elevated cTnI levels. Elevated cTnI levels were associated with inhospital mortality (P = .02), complicated clinical course (P<.001), and right ventricular dysfunction (P<.001). In patients with elevated cTnI levels, inhospital mortality (odds ratio [OR], 3.31; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.82-9.29), hypotension (OR, 7.37; 95% CI, 2.31-23.28), thrombolysis (OR, 5.71; 95% CI, 1.63-19.92), need for mechanical ventilation (OR, 5.00; 95% CI, 1.42-17.57), and need for inotropic support (OR, 3.02; 95% CI, 1.03-8.85) were more prevalent. The patients with elevated cTnI levels had more serious vital parameters (systolic blood pressure, pulse, and oxygen saturation) at ED presentation.

These findings strongly suggest that elevated troponin I is a valuable predictor of adverse outcomes in PE patients.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Elevated cTnI levels were associated with inhospital mortality (P = .02), complicated clinical course (P<.001), and right ventricular dysfunction (P<.001).
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other conditions can cause elevated troponin, the context of acute PE makes PE the most likely diagnosis. Other conditions like acute coronary syndrome or myocarditis were considered, but the study specifically focused on PE patients and the results strongly support the predictive value of troponin in this population.

The strong statistical significance (P<.001 for most outcomes) and large effect sizes (ORs ranging from 3.02 to 7.37) support the predictive value of cTnI in this context.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Elevated cTnI levels were associated with inhospital mortality (OR 3.31, P=0.02), complicated clinical course (P<0.001), and right ventricular dysfunction (P<0.001), with statistically significant odds ratios for adverse outcomes.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Alternative markers like D-dimer or B-type natriuretic peptide were not mentioned in the context, and the study specifically focused on cTnI's predictive value, which was supported by robust statistical evidence.
